speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE    STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at the opening of the session the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) made a statement, as a question of privilege, concerning a press story in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 5, referring to the Dixon-Speas report. I did not hear the earlier part of the hon. gentleman's statement, as I came into the house when his remarks were nearing conclusion.
In the course of his statement he quoted from the Winnipeg Free Press of November 5, part of which quotation was as follows:
Mrs. Konantz had seen the Dixon-Speas report and could understand why it could not be made public. She said it contained information which could not be given to C.P.A., T.C.A.'s main competitor.
Later in the day at the question period questions were asked on the same general subject matter by the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and in the course of these questions and answers I said I did not show the report to the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
The facts are that the hon. member for Winnipeg South came to my office, and among other subjects pressed me to do all I could to make sure that the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base did not move from Winnipeg, and asked me why I did not table the Dixon-Speas report. The Dixon-Speas report was on a table behind my desk where I had been working on it.

subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE    STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Kind of handy there.

subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE    STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
I explained to her why it could not be released. I pointed to it and indicated that four of the volumes contained almost exclusively material which could not be tabled because of its confidential nature, in that it gave detailed technical information that must remain confidential to the air line and that would be most useful to competitors.
The report was not removed from its place, nor was it opened or examined by Mrs. Konantz.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE    STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this question of privilege that was raised yesterday, and to which the Minister of Transport has now spoken, may I say there seems to be some question as to what the hon. member for Winnipeg South meant when she said, as reported, that she saw the report.
We note with interest the explanation given by the Minister of Transport. I understand that the hon. member for Winnipeg South will be returning from the United Nations to the House of Commons today or tomorrow, and we are prepared to wait until we hear from her before we consider whether any further steps should be taken.

speechtext:
1.	What is the total capital expenditure by the C.B.C. in relation to T.V. service for Flin Flon, Manitoba, and The Pas, Manitoba?
2.	What is the annual operational cost of this service?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COST OF TELEVISION SERVICE, FLIN FLON AND THE PAS, MAN.
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:
1.	Total capital expenditures to September 30, 1963 for: (i) Flin Flon, Manitoba, $251,431; <ii) The Pas, Manitoba, $116,831.
2.	The C.B.C. television station at Flin Flon is coupled with that at The Pas. They were planned as a complex and are operated jointly using television recording. The cost of television recording for a non-connected station is a national program charge, and is not included in the operating cost of these stations. There are no local program originations at either station.
A staff of four people is based at Flin Flon to handle the television recording and to provide maintenance service for both stations. Aside from the salaries of these four employees, operating costs are confined to those for building and technical maintenance, line costs, tube replacements, light, power, etc.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: *USE OF GOVERNMENT VEHICLES FOR PRIVATE ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
In its circular letter of November 25, 1954 (1954-24), the treasury board directed departments that the non-official use of government vehicles was prohibited unless the specific approval of the treasury board was obtained. In this regard the board in the same letter indicated that such approval might be granted in special cases where units are situated in isolated areas, and where there is no alternative transportation or the alternative transportation is most inadequate. Also, approval would be confined to such purposes as collection of mail, essential shopping, transportation of children to school, medical and dental attention, etc.
Employees of the following departments, who are working under the foregoing conditions, have been permitted to use departmental vehicles to attend to their personal needs and activities on the strength of individual authorities granted to their departments by the board:

The meaning of these expressions depends upon the context in which they are used. Legislative jurisdiction as to

holidays is divided between parliament and the provincial legislatures depending upon the subject matter and purpose of the legislation. Each may legislate with regard to holidays within its sphere of jurisdiction. Thus, the Interpretation Act of Canada defines holidays for the purposes of federal statutes and the interpretation act of Ontario defines holidays for the purposes of statutes of Ontario. Non-juridical days are set out in s. 43 of the Bills of Exchange Act. Days to be observed as holidays within the federal civil service are set out in s. 62 of the Civil Service Act. Days on which business may be transacted in provincial court and government offices depends upon provincial legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak at length on this question. The official opposition has taken the strongest exception to the manner of approach to United States investment in Canada. We have stated that the tax on dividends paid by corporations not having a degree of Canadian ownership does not meet the situation, and in its present form it is detrimental to investment in our country. However, having opposed these particular sections of the Income Tax Act and the other parties having generally given them support, there is no purpose in going over the ground again.
This is the last stage in the budget, a matter which goes back many months. It was a budget that was jerry built and has not stood up. After the budget was introduced there was a general demand for the removal of the Minister of Finance, but the government decided to get out of the budget practically completely and hold on to the minister. On the basis of what remains of the budget one can understand the description that was

Income Tax Act
given to the Canadian economy; "a rudderless mess". There was the budget of a few months ago. The promises which were made have not been carried out. My mind goes back to 1961 when the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) set out a financial and fiscal plan for Canada which was to be the salvation of the finances of this nation. He proposed four fiscal measures. The first of these was a temporary reduction in the rate of income tax. That was the promise made by the Liberal party in 1961. Instead of any reduction, the Canadian people today are being taxed approximately $250 million more than was the case when the present government came into office. Hon. gentlemen opposite said they would amend the Income Tax Act in this regard. They have done nothing to carry out this undertaking and their failure to do so cannot be explained on the ground that there is a deficit this year. When the undertaking was made in 1961 there was also a deficit, and the attitude then of the Liberal party was that there would be a reduction of income tax.
The second undertaking was that they would proceed to increase vocational training assistance. We have no quarrel with that, because it formed part of our own program. I believe, in this connection, the government should give consideration to encouraging adults to continue their education in parttime or night classes by allowing them to deduct tuition costs and expenses under the income tax. There are many thousands across Canada who today are attending night schools and there are many more who would attend if encouragement were given. Indeed, I think one of our primary purposes must be to expand and enlarge the vocational training plan which we brought into effect, so as to ensure that those who are middle aged and who wish to continue their education may have an opportunity to do so. At the same time, those who are younger in years and who desire to further their education by attending night schools should be entitled to the same deduction as if they were attending day schools.
The next proposal was a renewal program to be broadened and increased in the field of urban development. Finally, as part of the long term policy of the Liberal party, there was the medical health plan. This was the program of 1961 and 1962.
If we are to encourage the expansion of our country-and, at that time, the prime minister of the day said this was a necessary course to take-then tax cuts are necessary. But in place of carrying out the undertaking which was then given, the government has added extra burdens upon the people. In particular, I refer to the 11 per cent sales tax on building

materials and production machinery, a tax which should never have been imposed. Today, the rate of 4 per cent is in effect, and will be to the end of this fiscal year. I think there should be an immediate announcement made that the government will not press for the increase but will freeze the tax at the present rate. To sum up, the promises of 1961 in connection with income tax have followed the course of so many other promises which were made: they have not been carried into effect. Indeed, as far as taxation is concerned, instead of a reduction there has been a marked increase.
This is the background material. It indicates that the government has failed in the budget, or in what remains of the budget, to carry out the undertakings which were given. Having asked for reductions in taxation to meet the situation that exists in our country, following the lead of the United States in that regard in the message to congress by the President, I now come to one matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the house, and I intend to confine my remarks to it. It has to do with the subamendment which was accepted by the government last night. Its acceptance indicated a change of attitude on the part of the government. We had, from time to time, been demanding that there should be full consultation concerning all those matters which fall within the provincial arena. That has not been the attitude taken by the government, or the course which it has followed. The motion last evening was in the following terms:
That this house urges the government to carry out more fully the spirit of co-operative federalism and to consult with the provinces before announcing or undertaking programs which fall to any extent within provincial jurisdiction.
I do not intend to go into the circumstances surrounding the somersault last evening or the trickiness of the government's move. I shall accept it not as a tricky move designed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). I intend to regard it as a conversion. I am going to regard it as a change of attitude, and I think that is the fairest interpretation one could place on it. A review took place last evening of previous occasions when a similar course was followed, but there never was an occasion in Canadian history when a government, realizing it was facing a vote of want of confidence, decided, because it feared the result, to accept an amending motion. It simply means that from now on, however an amendment of non-confidence is moved, the government can say: we have more confidence than we think the opposition would have, and this being the case we are prepared to support the amendment in order to save ourselves.

They will never hear the last of their vote last evening.

we have the basic principle which should guide us in this particular instance:
When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.
It seems to me that this is what this amendment intends to do, and I would think that as far as the substance of it is concerned it is quite in order.
I go along with the argument submitted by some hon. members to the effect that there are technical difficulties or errors, but they are strictly technical. For example there is the fact that the amendment should have perhaps been brought in after subsection 2(b) rather than subsection 1(b); but if it were the will of the house the right hon. member could change his amendment at this time quite easily. This is not a substantial difficulty. Reference was also made to the fact that the amendment refers to paragraph 71 A, subsection 1(b) rather than to clause 16 of the bill itself. To my mind that is also a technicality and should not be taken into account by the Chair so as to declare the amendment out of order.
For these reasons I would rule that the amendment is acceptable in its present form.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some little while ago I was saying that I hoped, in view of the range of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, I might be given a little more licence than perhaps might be usual in introducing the remarks I should like to make with regard to the particular subject the Leader of the Opposition concentrated on toward the end of his comments. His criticism should really be examined in the context of the government's whole broad program for expanding the economy and reducing unemployment. He referred to a matter which went back, I think, to 1961 and to what, according to him, had been proposed at that time. If I may I should like to summarize very briefly the actions being taken, to date, in connection with the government's broad program for stimulating business activity and for creating new job opportunities.
1.	I should like, first, to mention the initial constructive action of the new Department of Industry to develop a new automobile policy. It is hoped that this policy will result in increased production of automobile parts in Canada to the amount of between $150 million and $200 million. This, of course, will create many thousands of new jobs.
2.	A municipal development and loan board has been established with a fund of $400 million. Agreements or arrangements have now been made with all the provinces and
Income Tax Act
the board is engaged in making loans. The increased construction activity which will result from this program should provide thousands of new jobs this winter and next winter.
3.	An Atlantic development board has been created, with a fund of $100 million. It is designed to strengthen the whole economic structure of the Atlantic area and in doing so it, also, will create many thousands of new jobs in that part of Canada.
4.	The technical and vocational program for training the unemployed has been expanded.
5.	Further encouragement has been given to municipal winter works incentive programs by raising the federal government's contribution from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of the direct payroll costs of approved projects in designated areas.
6.	The federal government has speeded up its own construction programs in designated areas-or will speed them up-this winter.
7.	A new program has been approved to encourage the employment of older workers. This is provided for in the part of the budget to which the right hon. gentleman referred. The federal government will pay 50 per cent of the monthly wages paid to workers over 45 who have been out of work for a consecutive period of nine months, up to a maximum of $75 per month.
8.	A bonus of $500 will be paid to the first purchasers of winter built houses.
9.	The necessary funds have been provided to permit the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to finance an expanded house building program during this coming winter.
10.	Generous tax incentives have been approved-I should say we hope they will now be approved-to encourage new manufacturing and processing businesses in areas of slower growth and persistent unemployment. This is one of the matters under discussion in the bill which is now before the house.
11.	Incentives are provided for industries with a degree of Canadian ownership to expand anywhere in Canada. This, also, is in the bill before us.
We are very hopeful that this new broad program will be successful. We think it will be. We are very hopeful that the particular program designed to assist unemployed workers over 45 years of age will be successful. The right hon. gentleman referred once or twice to the budget, and I should like to remind him that this was provided for in the budget. It is something about which all of us on this side are very proud. It is the first time a special program of this kind has been developed to help re-establish as useful members of society men in middle life who have been out of work for a long time.

Income Tax Act
I should also like to say that we are receiving encouraging reports about the program for stimulating winter house building and that the original estimates of what might be achieved under this program are now being revised upwards.
The policy for stimulating economic activity in areas of slower growth is a new one for Canada although similar policies have worked successfully in Britain and in most of the countries of western Europe. The government is hopeful that the generous incentives provided for in the bill which is now before the house will encourage new manufacturing and processing businesses to establish themselves in these areas. These are the areas where unemployment has been exceptionally high and where it has persisted for some years. The new policy is aimed directly at the solution of this evil. This policy for stimulating activity in areas of slower growth is, as I have indicated, only one item, though an important item, in the broad and comprehensive program which has been developed by the government. Though it has worked successfully in the United Kingdom and in various countries of Europe, as I said a moment ago, it has not previously been tried in Canada and we believe it is high time that it should be. It is time a real effort was made to revive and reinvigorate these areas of slow growth where the level of unemployment has been high and chronic.
Conservative spokesmen have opposed this new policy on three grounds. First, they have opposed it because it is a new and untried idea, at least in Canada. We all know that some people do not like new ideas.

That was an interesting remark but I did not quite get its implication. I should like to raise another matter which seems to me of paramount importance in connection with this particular criticism. We Liberals believe, and I am sure some members of other parties believe, that the federal government must take some responsibility for the level of economic activity and the opportunities for employment throughout the whole of Canada. This should not and cannot be left to the ten provincial governments acting independently. We were elected to do our very best to improve conditions in Canada and to take whatever action may be needed to provide jobs for the people who need them so badly. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that we cannot shirk that responsibility by saying that it is the responsibilty of the provinces, as was implied by the Leader of the Opposition.
The third criticism of this whole policy for stimulating economic activity in areas of slower growth and high and chronic unemployment is that the areas that have been singled out for special help should have been designated in some other way. No one has said just how this should have been done; presumably no one has any idea of how this should be done or he would have suggested it.
As I explained in the house on November 6, and the reference is Hansard, page 4473, the criteria for the selection of designated areas have been based on the employment and unemployment record for the summer months rather than the annual average, in

order to avoid undue emphasis on winter unemployment in areas where the main problem is not of a seasonal character. At that time I reviewed in detail the criteria for the establishment of a designated area and I also pointed out that provision had been made for flexibility in altering the boundaries of designated areas and for adding new national employment service areas as soon as or if they fulfil, and I hope they do not, the criteria of eligibility. I hope they do not, because that might suggest we were going to have substantial unemployment in other parts of the country, which we would all deplore.
Opposition spokesmen have concentrated their attacks with regard to designated areas on questioning whether one particular area, namely Brantford, should have been included in the list. My colleague, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), dealt with this question in detail on October 16 and his remarks will be found in Hansard at page 3651. As he pointed out, representations from all 35 areas designated, including Brantford, have registered only satisfaction with having been so designated.
I think I might also point out that of the total of 31 surplus manpower areas declared by the previous government, 11 are identical with the present list of designated areas and in a number of others there is some degree of overlapping. I think some hon. members may have got the impression that the definition of a designated area is something new and very different. I should like to summarize the definition of a surplus manpower area that was developed previously and show how closely the new definition follows it.
Under the surplus manpower definition it was provided, first, that areas with a labour force of 10,000 or over must be classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category for 75 per cent or more of the summer months, May to October, 1953 to 1960; also, industrial employment must have declined. Under the first requirement of the definition of a designated area the area must be classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months-in the earlier one it was 75 per cent-May to October during the past eight years, and it has experienced an employment increase of less than one half the national average over the same period.
There are alternatives. The first one under the surplus manpower definition provides that areas with a labour force of 10,000 must have been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus market for 50 per cent or more of the summer months, 1953 to 1960;
Income Tax Act
also, industrial employment must have deteriorated over this period. Under the new definition of a designated area the alternative is that it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one third or more of the summer months, May to October, during the past eight years, and it has experienced an employment decrease over the same period.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have been arguing about two definitions that are very similar, and for the life of me I cannot understand what all the fuss has been about.

I am really very pleased the hon. member for Ontario has asked me this question because it gives me the opportunity to range a little farther than perhaps I should have been able to do otherwise. When you get down

Before the last budget, I considered whether or not the whole principle of the way it has been done for generations under our system should be changed. I wondered at that time, and I still wonder, whether it would be practical to have a series of public discussions ahead of time to get the views and suggestions of various people, not so that the government could duck this responsibility, because in the last analysis under our system the government must produce a budget and must accept responsibility for it, but mainly to get the benefit of other people's ideas.
I have been thinking about this recently, as I am sure other hon. members have been. It seems to me that at the moment the best we can do is to invite the principal organizational groups to put forward their ideas, let the government have the benefit of their ideas at an early stage and not have these briefs and representations coming along after the main budget proposals have been pretty well decided. This year we have asked that these representations or proposals be made to the government, preferably in December but in any event by the end of January.

Therefore I feel it would be only common sense to diversify the western Canadian economy as much as possible. I believe the farmers have done this to a large extent in certain areas, and I would think one way to do this would be to encourage, in every possible way, the establishment of industry in western Canada.
I simply cannot understand the ignoring of western interests because if such a policy were successful, and if it holds the high hopes that the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Finance have indicated, it would strengthen immeasurably the western economy, and the economy of the whole of Canada. I think that this situation highlights above all others the basic weakness of this legislation, in which it fails to provide for consultation with the provinces, because the question of these designated areas is of the utmost importance.
After all this talk we have heard about cooperative federalism, it would seem to me the first thing the government would do, or would want to do, is bring the provinces into the picture. Had they done this they would not be in the mess they are now in, relative to the city of Brantford.

Some few days ago the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) made a factual and well constructed speech, and went to considerable pains to point out that the legislation such as we have been considering in regard to designated areas had been successfully used in European countries, and more particularly in Great Britain. In fact I think she pointed out at that time that they had gone very much farther than we had attempted to go in this country.
I would certainly corroborate her statement in this regard because I had some experience, some years ago in England, in the interests of the company with which I am associated, of trying to develop export business. At that time the British government offered very interesting incentives to have us start an operation in Britain, but the point was that this operation had to be established in the depressed areas. From memory I recall they offered to build a plant to our specifications, and lease it to us if we would establish in a certain area in Wales, and I recall, as the hon. lady mentioned, that there were extremely attractive incentives for the establishment of industry in Northern Ireland and in various other places in Great Britain.
But the point is that there was no premium for industry to establish in London. There was no premium for industry to establish on the rich and wealthy south coast, nor I believe in the industrial midlands. That is exactly the point I want to try and make and stress here today. There should not be 28902-5-300i
Income Tax Act
any subsidy for industry to establish in any community that borders on the perimeter of one of the richest, most industrialized and progressive areas in the whole of Canada.
As I tried to indicate earlier, I have the highest personal regard for the Minister of Finance, and I am sure he will not take any undue offence, but can you imagine his consternation if he woke up one morning and found that an adjoining constituency to his riding in Davenport had been declared a depressed area? One may say that obviously in a metropolitan area such as Toronto a riding could not possibly be made a designated area without including the whole metropolitan area. That is the point I am trying to make here.
The distance between Galt and Brantford is some 15 miles. This is considerably less than is encompassed in metropolitan Toronto, and I suggest most strongly that the government cannot proffer special treatment to one community without damaging the adjacent communities. This is particularly true when the proposed designated area has no physical handicaps, as compared to its immediate neighbours. Its location is comparable. It has comparable transportation facilities. Its power rates are comparable and, although I have not gone into this, I do not see any reason that its assessment or taxing structure would be out of line with the surrounding communities. The climate is the same. There is no difference in terrain. The designated area is centrally located, and there simply is not any reason that can be explained to me why Brantford cannot stand on its own feet.
Now, if I have seemed unduly critical of Brantford, that was not my intention. I do not blame the officials of Brantford for taking advantage of this unexpected windfall. They have done what anybody else would have done under the circumstances, and I do not blame them at all for it. They simply cannot afford to look a gift horse of this kind in the mouth. This is the kind of gift horse they would gladly see stay on the government payroll in perpetuity, and I believe the minister has certain experience along that line.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to relate to the house the story of a certain community in Waterloo South, and I speak of the town of Hespeler. I might explain that back in 1958 it was a one-industry town dominated by and dependant by and large on the huge Dominion Woollens plant that had operated there for years. This plant had thousands of employees during the world war, and up until 1958 it employed some 600 or 700 persons. Then, in April of that year, the plant closed down putting those 600 or 700 persons

Income Tax Act
completely out of work and with apparently no possibility of getting work in that community.
This in a community of 4,000 people, so you can see, Mr. Speaker, the crisis which faces them. This action left 11 acres of factory space empty. I am not going to dwell at length on this, but these people did not come crying to the government asking for government subsidies. They got off their fat seats and went out and brought industry into the community, and today the floor space in that plant is filled. New industries have come in during the last few months and established themselves, and the community is now in a stronger position than it has ever been in the past. I use that simply as an illustration of the initiative shown by this one small community.
I do not want to appear unduly critical of Brantford, as I say, or make odious comparisons, but I think that what this small community has accomplished is obvious. I feel the Minister of Industry, and perhaps the Minister of Finance who has been defending this bill, in making this decision to designate Brantford as a retarded area have been the victims of their own statistics. Statistics have their place and their value, but at best serve merely as a guide line. Certainly they have to be understood. Looking back into the past it seems only a short time ago when the Liberal party during the last election had a full head of steam and were in full flight. The whole country reverberated with their slogan: "Take a stand for tomorrow".

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Someone says hear, hear. To me that slogan indicated an interest in the future; that some forward-looking stand would be taken. The Minister of Industry is now looking eight years backwards. He is not looking to the future. He has made his judgment on stale and rancid statistics which are today meaningless.
What does the future hold for Galt, Kitchener, Preston, Guelph and that whole area that it does not hold for Brantford? There is a $13 million Massey-Harris plant being built there, and it will be interesting to note whether this plant will qualify for these subsidies. From what I have said I do not mean to suggest that Brantford has been without any problems. One of the serious problems which has confronted that community has been the fact that the production of some of the major industries has been rather seasonal in nature, which has resulted in higher than normal lay-offs during the summer. This is where the statistics have been deceptive. I

suggest that the subsidization of new industry to establish itself in a community will not correct this situation. I am afraid I never did know what was to be the ultimate function of the new Department of Industry, but I respectfully suggest that the minister or a representative from his department might have consulted with these particular industries to explore the possibility of their levelling out their peaks and their valleys of production. That might indeed have proven fruitful, and this should have been done before the minister committed himself so hastily to a policy of subsidizing industry in an area which really does not need it and for which there is no justification. Government speakers from time to time have admitted that this particular part of the legislation is discriminatory, and they have tried to justify this discrimination. Coming from an adjoining area I feel that this is vicious discrimination which has already proved damaging to adjacent communities.
I do not want to take too much time in quoting from the press, but I have before me a copy of the Brantford Expositor of Wednesday, November 6. There is an article headed. "City sends stream of mail to new industry prospects" and it goes on to say:
Brantford may be a "designated area" industrially-indicative of slow economic growth-but it is fast taking advantage of the label.
A stream of mail-outlining the tax benefits of locating new industries in Brantford has been shot out of acting industrial commissioner Harry Richards' office to all and any industry of which he can think.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that speaks for itself.
And now what of the future? In fact, what of the present? If hon. members look at the copies of the Canada Labour Gazette they will find statistics given relative to the labour supply. They will find that in the month of September certain things happened. In the September issue there is a table showing the classification of labour market areas, and it is broken down into areas of substantial labour surplus and moderate labour surplus, showing the approximate balance and labour shortage. In September Brantford was in the approximate balance group, as was Kitchener and Guelph. Looking back to August the situation was the same. Going back further Brantford is shown in some situations as an area of moderate surplus labour. At the same time Galt, Kitchener and other areas in that vicinity are also shown as moderate surplus areas. I have been trying to point out that Brantford suffers from no natural hazards or handicaps common to other sections of the area. These other communities have no natural advantages, certainly no substantial advantages, over Brantford, and as I said earlier

I feel strongly that this is a matter of the application of public funds.
I also said earlier that I agree with the general principle of this legislation and what it was supposed to accomplish, but I think that this legislation would have been infinitely stronger and the government would have been greatly strengthened had they provided in the legislation consultation and co-operation with the provinces. I suggest that had they done so, and had they consulted with the Ontario government, they would not find themselves in this particular difficulty with regard to Ontario today.
I should now like to refer to another clause in the bill. I believe it is 71.A. (3). At any rate, it has to do with the capital cost of machinery. I will not read this particular paragraph, but having read Hansard in connection with it I feel there has been considerable confusion as to its meaning. I gather from the statement made by the minister that the direct effect will be to ensure that industries establishing themselves in designated areas must supply themselves with new machinery at least to the extent of 95 per cent. I have read the comments of the Minister of Finance on this and I can understand the point he is making when he says he does not want people bringing in second hand machinery to compete with established firms. X think there is a certain validity about this point. I also noticed the comments of the Minister of Industry in this regard to the effect that it is to precisely to avoid the likelihood of businesses which, rather than expanding and creating a new operation, merely shift their centre of operations from one area to another, that a provision of this kind is needed.
I think the possibility of such a thing happening is much more apparent than real. It might be possible in certain light industries, for example the needle trades, for all concerned to pack up over the week end and move to another location. But-apparently, the minister does not appreciate the problems which would be involved in moving a heavy or a medium sized industry. It would take months. There would be great difficulty about maintaining production, providing for continuity of supplies to customers and so on. Formidable problems would be presented and from my own experience I can say that no company would go to such trouble and expense unless the move were part of a long-range plan not likely to be predicated upon tax incentives of a few years duration, such as this one.
Nevertheless, I feel that the clause providing for 95 per cent new equipment as contained in this legislation is unrealistic. In my opinion some lesser figure would meet the
Income Tax Act
requirement of the Minister of Finance. I see that an amendment was moved to reduce the figure to 25 per cent, but this was not acceptable to the government. I should like to suggest that 50 per cent would not be unreasonable and that if, in conjunction with it, there were a provision specifying that this 50 per cent be Canadian made, I think we would have something which would be both workable and beneficial. Thus, when a new company sought to establish itself in a designated area under this legislation the effect would be to stimulate other industry in this country. I believe this would not be far out of line with the objectives expressed by the Minister of Finance himself, namely to have more manufacturing done in Canada.
My own experience provides some basis for this suggestion, that 50 per cent of the machinery should be Canadian made. The company with which I am associated has, in the last two or three years, undertaken a large capital expenditure program involving certain heavy equipment which could not be obtained in Canada. But in every case where this equipment was built for us we insisted on having the manufacturer in the United States assign as much work as was possible to be done in Canada, out of Canadian materials and parts. It is surprising what can be accomplished in this direction if a determined effort is made. Thus I have found that even when machinery and equipment cannot be purchased complete in Canada, a 50 per cent Canadian content is not at all unreasonable. Moreover, there are many companies working in Canada today under licence agreements enabling them to bring in certain essentials and use certain designs, though the majority of the work is done and completed in Canada.
For these reasons I say that the percentage of Canadian content I have suggested would not be unreasonable. On the contrary it would be very practicable and I respectfully suggest that the minister give this proposal serious consideration and incorporate it into the legislation now before us.

I remember, too, the speeches he made to the people of Canada over the television and radio, and so on, before June 18, 1962. As I said before: Oh, the exhortations of those who are without sin. At the time the television broadcast was made, subsequent to the imposition of those surcharges on June 24, 1962, people across Canada laughed at a man who had built such an image, only to destroy himself in such a short time.

In- reading the amendment over and over again, and taking into account our past experience and the statements made yesterday, I cannot help but think that the political parties have only one objective at this time and it is to try and make the people of Quebec believe that they have realized the problem facing that province and that they are prepared to settle it, although they have really understood nothing of the present problem of federal-provincial relations.
Indeed, the crux of the problem is on taxation reform. And it is precisely that matter which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition would not discuss last night.
The problem really concerns taxation reform between the federal government and the provinces, rather than an amendment like the one moved by the Leader of the
Division
Opposition, under which the federal government would first designate some regions which in turn, through their provincial government would ask the federal government to accept them.
I think that it is a way to evade the question, a way to throw a smokescreen over the true problem. Well, we will not be a party to this evasive action by the old line political parties.
Mr. Speaker, we do not wish to take any part in endeavours to divert attention from the real problem and this is why we will not fall into the snare set for us when we are told that it is in order to protect the rights and privileges demanded by the provinces.
We feel that this amendment is no solution to the real problem. We would like the problem to be really considered from the point of view which we have suggested, that is to give each province the means to look after its own affairs and not always treat the matter lightly by submitting amendments as it is now done.
The amendment, I must add, is very complicated. No matter how much we would consider and reconsider it from all angles, in our opinion, it remains just as complicated.
I wonder who could find a meaning to it. It it had been explained to us, perhaps we could express our views, but I must say that we will vote against it at this time.
Provincial autonomy would no more be respected if the municipal authorities were asked to voice their feelings to the federal government. Municipalities being creatures of the provincial governments have no business, in our opinion, to deal with the central government; that is up to the provinces.
